title: BMI-era songs, Ellington's 1960s records, Mercer Ellington
summary: They talk about BMI tunes and Ellington's recordings and Duke's treatment of Mercer.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: All those records... You know, that's when BMI started, and they started tunes like... [SINGS]... "I Hear a Rhapsody," or "Darn That Dream"... [SINGS] A lot of beautiful things came out! "Eye On A Windy Hill." A lot of great tunes. Guys that that never had a chance were
Rowles - 51

suddenly hearing their music. And there was some beautiful, beautiful stuff. And Duke used to play... He used to buy the stocks, and he'd take the third alto part and give it to the baritone player, and get the same sound.
Harry, yeah. They had a lot of pop tunes in their repertoire at that time, too.
Mmm-hmm..
Stuff that they often didn't record...
I love those records of Ellington, '65, '66.

Yeah. Where he does "Danke Schoen." I like "Danke Schoen" -- he does a nice job. I was at a couple of those sessions when they made those. Out in Long Island, some studio way out on the Island. You know, the guys were...
It's all Billy Strayhorn.

Yeah, Billy, and Mercer did a couple of them. And I remember how mean Duke was. I mean, Duke usually wasn't like that. But Mercer, when they pulled out one of Mercer's things, and they started running throughgh it, and Duke said, "Who wrote this?" -- and he really put him down in front of, you know, the band and whoever was there. He would never have done that to anybody else. But Mercer... Did you read Mercer's book?
I have the book. I have never read it.
Well, it's interesting, because he speaks very frankly
Rowles - 52
about, you know... He loved his father, but at the same time, they had a lot of difficult times.
Like Gary Crosby's book, huh?

Well, not quite like that, but... I think Mercer says that his father didn't really want him to be a musician; he wanted him to be something else, an engineer or a scientist or something. And Mercer insisted on going into music. Duke always felt that he didn't have any particularly great talent, which may well be true. But in later years, of course, he came to rely a lot on Mercer, when Mercer was really the road manager and Mercer was the guy who always had to, you know...
Give him a shot?

Or fire somebody. Although, as we all know, Duke never fired anybody, but make them quit, you know... There's some beautiful stuff... We just talked about records that got destroyed. But all those Treasury broadcasts that the Ellington band used to do in the Forties, they're all coming out on LP. There's a guy who is putting out 47 LPs, and it's up to thirty-something now. But on those, you'll hear the band play a lot of things that they never recorded commercially. Things like "Don't You Know I Care?" and... There's a beautiful thing, I forget which it is now, which has a duet between Carney and Otto Hardwick. Now, Hardwick
Rowles - 53
never got to so much, but he had such a sweet saxophone sound, different from Johnny's.
Is he still living?
No. He died a long time ago. He was one of the oldest guys in the band.
Yeah, I know. I can still see that guitar player going to sleep.
